items.explanation: 'Protection' was the official fig leaf; the real drivers were suspicion of divided loyalties, press hysteria about sabotage, and racist propaganda — which is why no similar roundup hit German or Italian Americans.
options: A. Suspicions of divided loyalty in California
B. Press reports of Japanese-American sabotage
C. A need to protect Japanese Americans in camps
D. Racist portrayals in films and magazines
items.stem: Japanese-American internment began for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Suspicion of divided loyalty in California really was a driver — West Coast politicians and the press stoked fears that Japanese-Americans were loyal to Japan. This was a real cause, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Press reports of Japanese-American sabotage really did feed the panic — though no sabotage was ever documented, the hysteria was a real driver of internment. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. 'Protection' of Japanese-Americans was the government's official fig leaf; the real drivers were suspicion, press hysteria, and racism. That no similar roundup hit German or Italian Americans shows protection was not the motive.
option_explanations.D: Racist portrayals in films and magazines really did feed the climate for internment — anti-Japanese propaganda was a genuine driver. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Pearl Harbor, visible difference, and venomous propaganda all fed hatred; the Bataan Death March came in 1942 and the U.S. government revealed the details only in January 1944 — it could not have caused wartime hatred from the start.
options: A. The bombing of Pearl Harbor
B. Visible physical difference
C. Outrage over the Bataan Death March from the start
D. Venomous press and film portrayals
items.stem: Which was NOT a reason for wartime hatred of the Japanese?

option_explanations.A: The Pearl Harbor bombing really did fuel wartime hatred of the Japanese — it was the immediate trigger. This was a real cause, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Visible physical difference really did feed the hatred — unlike German or Italian Americans, Japanese-Americans were racially distinguishable, which made scapegoating easier. This was a real cause, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. The Bataan Death March happened in 1942, and the U.S. government revealed the details only in January 1944 — it could not have caused wartime hatred 'from the start.'
option_explanations.D: Venomous press and film portrayals really did feed the hatred — anti-Japanese propaganda was relentless. This was a real cause, not the exception.

items.explanation: Germany was divided into four occupation zones, not handed to Moscow; critics' real complaints were Yalta's blessing of Soviet domination in Eastern Europe, the vague promise of Japanese war entry, and Roosevelt's failing health.
options: A. The USSR got control of most of Germany
B. The Soviets' Japan pledge was vague
C. Roosevelt was visibly near death
D. Soviet-liberated nations stayed under Moscow
items.stem: Later critics attacked the Yalta Conference for all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. Germany was divided into four occupation zones (American, British, French, Soviet) — the USSR never got control of most of Germany. Critics' real complaints were about Eastern Europe, the vague Japan pledge, and Roosevelt's failing health.
option_explanations.B: The Soviets' vague pledge to enter the war against Japan really was a criticism of Yalta — critics attacked the concessions Roosevelt made to secure it. This was a real complaint, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Roosevelt's visibly failing health really was a criticism — critics argued he was too ill to bargain hard with Stalin. This was a real complaint, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Soviet-liberated nations staying under Moscow really was a criticism — Yalta's blessing of Soviet domination in Eastern Europe was the critics' central grievance. This was a real complaint, not the exception.

items.explanation: Depression-era America was absorbed in domestic recovery, and the Nye Committee's 'merchants of death' verdict made intervention politically toxic — both kept America aloof from Hitler's rise.
options: A. America focused on Pacific diplomacy
B. America was absorbed in domestic problems
C. The Nye Committee soured Americans on intervention
D. Both B and C
items.stem: America did little to check Hitler in the 1930s because

option_explanations.A: America did not focus on Pacific diplomacy in the 1930s — Washington stayed aloof from both theaters. The Pacific was not the reason America ignored Hitler.
option_explanations.B: America really was absorbed in domestic problems — the Depression consumed the nation's political energy. This was a genuine cause, but only half the answer.
option_explanations.C: The Nye Committee really did sour Americans on intervention — its 'merchants of death' verdict made foreign entanglement politically toxic. This was a genuine cause, but only half the answer.
option_explanations.D: Correct — both B and C. Depression-era America was absorbed in domestic recovery, and the Nye Committee's 'merchants of death' verdict made intervention politically toxic. Together they kept America aloof from Hitler's rise.

items.explanation: Baseball, movies, and big bands thrived on the home front; auto racing died — gasoline and rubber rationing made it impossible for most of the war.
options: A. Auto racing
B. Professional baseball
C. Movies
D. Big band concerts
items.stem: Wartime Americans flocked to all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. Auto racing died during the war — gasoline and rubber rationing made it impossible for most of the conflict, while baseball, movies, and big bands thrived on the home front.
option_explanations.B: Professional baseball really did thrive on the home front — it was wartime America's pastime. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Movies really did thrive on the home front — wartime audiences flocked to theaters. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Big band concerts really did thrive on the home front — swing was the soundtrack of the war years. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: The release announces 'an atomic bomb' -- 'the harnessing of the basic power of the universe' -- and justifies its use as repayment for Pearl Harbor and a means to end the war. It is a public announcement and defense of a revolutionary weapon, issued hours after Hiroshima; it declares no new war, no surrender, and addresses no warning to Moscow.
options: A. to declare war on Japan
B. to announce and justify the use of a revolutionary new weapon
C. to announce Japan's surrender
D. to secretly warn the Soviet Union
items.stem: Truman issued this press release primarily to
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

President Truman's August 1945 announcement told the nation that an American plane had dropped a single bomb on Hiroshima with explosive force equal to more than 20,000 tons of TNT — a weapon, he said, that would shorten the agony of war.
—After President Harry Truman's press release, August 6, 1945

option_explanations.A: The release did not declare war on Japan — the United States had been at war with Japan since December 1941. Declaring war was four years in the past.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The release announces 'an atomic bomb' — 'the harnessing of the basic power of the universe' — and justifies its use as repayment for Pearl Harbor and a means to shorten the war. It is a public announcement and defense of a revolutionary weapon, issued hours after Hiroshima.
option_explanations.C: The release did not announce Japan's surrender — Japan fought on for nine more days, surrendering only after Nagasaki and the Soviet entry. No surrender is announced here.
option_explanations.D: The release contains no secret warning to the Soviet Union — it is a public announcement addressed to the American people about the bomb and its justification, not a message to Moscow.

items.explanation: At Midway (June 1942) American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers -- the core of Japan's offensive striking power -- at the cost of one American carrier. Japan never recovered the initiative; the victory is routinely called the turning point of the Pacific war. Tokyo was not captured, the war ran three more years, and the merchant fleet survived.
options: A. it destroyed four Japanese carriers, crippling Japan's offensive naval power
B. it resulted in the capture of Tokyo
C. it ended the Pacific war immediately
D. it sank the entire Japanese merchant fleet
items.stem: The Battle of Midway proved decisive in the Pacific war because it
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

President Truman's August 1945 announcement told the nation that an American plane had dropped a single bomb on Hiroshima with explosive force equal to more than 20,000 tons of TNT — a weapon, he said, that would shorten the agony of war.
—After President Harry Truman's press release, August 6, 1945

option_explanations.A: Correct. At Midway (June 1942) American carriers sank four Japanese fleet carriers — the core of Japan's offensive striking power — at the cost of one American carrier. Japan never recovered the initiative; the victory is routinely called the turning point of the Pacific war.
option_explanations.B: Midway did not capture Tokyo — Tokyo fell only with Japan's surrender in 1945. Midway was a naval battle, not a landing on the Japanese home islands.
option_explanations.C: Midway did not end the Pacific war — three more years of brutal island fighting followed. It was the turning point, not the end.
option_explanations.D: Midway did not sink Japan's merchant fleet — it destroyed four fleet carriers. The merchant fleet survived and was strangled later by the submarine campaign.

items.explanation: The release mentions Pearl Harbor, the bomb's power ('more power than 20,000 tons of T.N.T.'), and 'even more powerful forms... in development.' It says nothing of the Soviet Union -- which declared war on Japan on August 8, between the two bombings, an event some historians rank with the bombs in forcing surrender. The omission frames the victory as America's weapon alone.
options: A. Any mention of Pearl Harbor
B. Any description of the bomb's power
C. Any reference to future bomb production
D. Any mention of the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan
items.stem: Notably absent from Truman's announcement is
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

President Truman's August 1945 announcement told the nation that an American plane had dropped a single bomb on Hiroshima with explosive force equal to more than 20,000 tons of TNT — a weapon, he said, that would shorten the agony of war.
—After President Harry Truman's press release, August 6, 1945

option_explanations.A: Pearl Harbor is mentioned in the announcement — Truman frames the bomb as repayment for Pearl Harbor. It is not absent.
option_explanations.B: The bomb's power is described — 'more power than 20,000 tons of T.N.T.' It is not absent.
option_explanations.C: Future bomb production is referenced — the release speaks of 'even more powerful forms' in development. It is not absent.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The release says nothing of the Soviet Union's entry into the war against Japan — which came on August 8, between the two bombings, and which some historians rank with the bombs in forcing surrender. The omission frames the victory as America's weapon alone.
